newsitem.title: USA: It's great to be home, says U.S. astronaut.
newsitem.headline: It's great to be home, says U.S. astronaut.

text.p: U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger said on Saturday he was feeling great after returning to Earth on space shuttle Atlantis from a four-month stay on Russia's troubled Mir space station.
The 42-year-old astronaut said after 132 days in space he was strong enough to walk from the shuttle after its landing on Saturday.
"I felt way better than I thought I would feel. I still feel physically strong," he said in an interview recorded by NASA. "It's amazing to me. I really thought it would be a lot tougher."
Atlantis had swooped out of a partly cloudy sky and touched down at 9:27 a.m. EDT (1327 GMT) at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
During its nine-day mission, the shuttle docked with Russia's Mir space station to collect Linenger and drop off his replacement, British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale.
"Feeling great and good to be home," Linenger told mission control soon after the landing. He rode back to Earth in a reclining chair to cushion him from the pull of gravity.
The astronaut said he had missed his family and the simple things about life on Earth during his tour of duty aboard Mir.
"I'll tell you man, just fresh air feels good and the breeze in my face," he said.
Soon after landing, Linenger was reunited with his 18-month old son and his wife Kathryn, who is expecting their second child in June.

Space agency chief Daniel Goldin brought gifts for the astronaut to give to his family: a bouquet of yellow and purple tulips for his wife; a small teddy bear in a NASA sweatshirt for his son; and a rattle for his unborn child.
"He couldn't go out to a store in space," Goldin explained to reporters.
Linenger, a medical doctor and Navy captain, was determined to walk off the shuttle under his own power, despite NASA's preference for him to be carried off.
Only one of the four astronauts returning from long missions to Mir has admitted to being carried off.

Linenger had a rigorous exercise programme on Mir to ward off the debilatating effects of weightlessness. His workouts included running two hours a day on a treadmill, doing squats and using expander cords.
Although the exercise programme was disrupted by problems aboard the space station, Linenger appeared well, standing throughout the five-minute NASA interview and also holding his son for a while.
Space agency officials expected Linenger would fully regain his "Earth legs" within a few days and be able to return to work in a month.
Months of space travel can cause bones to weaken and muscles to waste away. Astronauts often feel weak and woozy on their return to Earth.
Linenger's four-month stay on Mir was marred by a serious fire, life support problems and a near collision with an unmanned cargo craft.
The mission ended on a high note when on April 29 Linenger and his Russian commander, Vasily Tsibliev, stepped outside on a spacewalk, the first by an American from Mir.
Linenger's stay in space was the second-longest mission by an American astronaut, surpassed only by Shannon Lucid's 188-day mission to Mir in 1996.
Atlantis, which blasted off on May 15, spent five days docked at the Russian orbital outpost.
In addition to swapping astronauts, the shuttle carried to Mir two tons of much-needed supplies and equipment, including an oxygen generator and gear to plug cooling system leaks.
Foale, the fifth U.S. astronaut to live and work on Mir, is to return to Earth in September.

The shuttle's touchdown was delayed 90 minutes by cloudy skies at the Florida spaceport. Flight controllers in Houston watched the weather until the last minute before giving Atlantis permission to land.
